Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback

Thomson Yen1,*, Gilbert Yang1,*, Naimeng Ye1,*, Minghui Chen1,*, Dong Xia1, Tianyi Shen2, Yechan Jeon1, Yaqin Chen3, Daksh Mittal1, Fangyu Wu1, Hongseok Namkoong1 1Decision, Risk, and Operations Division, Columbia Business School, 2University of California, Santa Barbara, 3Northwestern University *Equal contribution
Abstract

Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within KK sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models’ iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.

1 Introduction

Multi-turn interaction with feedback is a fundamental pattern of machine learning, driving classical paradigms including multi-armed bandits (Auer et al., 2002), active learning (Settles, 2009), and reinforcement learning (Sutton & Barto, 2018). Recently, this same principle has catalyzed much of the progress in large language models (LLMs), underpinning advances in test-time compute (Snell et al., 2024), automatic prompt optimization (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025), and agentic systems (Park et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Yet a striking disconnect has emerged between how these systems operate and how they are evaluated. Even as modern methods (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023) and environments (Wang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025) center on iterative refinement, the community still ranks models primarily by Pass@K (Chen et al., 2021), a strictly feedback-blind metric.

We argue that relying solely on feedback-blind evaluation is insufficient for developing agentic systems—it may reward the wrong behaviors and obscure the right ones. For example, consider a coding agent: the user issues an initial request, the agent proposes an edit, the user responds with targeted critiques, and the agent revises. This loop of proposal, feedback, and revision is the dominant pattern of agent usage today, with applications extending far beyond coding. Yet Pass@K is blind to whether an agent can excel in this sequential decision-making loop. This blind spot hides failure modes and undervalues models that successfully improve through iteration.

In this work, we quantify a model’s ability to improve under sequential feedback by measuring it along a new axis, which we name Seq@K. Seq@K measures whether a model solves a task within KK attempts when it receives feedback after each failed attempt. Ranking models by Pass@K implicitly assumes that a model that is accurate in one turn also uses feedback well. We show that this assumption often breaks down. We evaluate Seq@K on coding (MBPP Pro, HumanEval Pro (Yu et al., 2025)), complex instruction following (AdvancedIF (He et al., 2025)), domain reasoning (CLBench DKR (Dou et al., 2026)), and medical benchmarks (HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025)). Our results reveal how model rankings, cost frontiers, and failure modes change when models are allowed to revise their work based on feedback.

Our contributions and key empirical insights are structured around three primary questions:

  1. 1.

    Model Selection & Cost Dynamics: Model rankings can change between evaluations based on Pass@K and Seq@K. We demonstrate (a) the benefit of Seq@K by showing that it leads to better and more cost-efficient model as calibration metric, (b) Pass@K can understate or overstate differences in model capability under sequential feedback. (c) Seq@K often exposes superior Pareto frontier at deployment than that of Pass@K and (d) how Seq@K tracks a different capability from Pass@K (Section 5.1).

  2. 2.

    Uncovering Revision Patterns: Beyond reporting Seq@K, we further analyze the way in which models revise their attempts: (a) models can differ in when they gain, with some gaining most on the first retry and others on later attempts, (b) revisions do not always address the feedback, and some models resubmit the same attempt unchanged, and (c) even revisions that address all of the feedback can fail by breaking requirements that passed before (Section 5.2).

  3. 3.

    Diagnosing the Feedback Loop: Seq@K also helps diagnose the feedback itself. We show (a) the usefulness of informative feedback depends on both the benchmark and the model capability, (b) critiques written with the grading rubric tend to help models repair far more failed requirements, and (c) summarizing the previous attempts can lower success rate, so how the history is kept should be reported along with Seq@K (Section 5.3).

2 Related Work

Refinement from feedback.

A line of related work considers having a model reasoning and revising in response to critique or execution feedback as methods to improve agent performance (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024). Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) is the closet to our setting by considering agent’s reasoning on top of binary pass/fail signal or results on self-generated test cases. In contrast, our work centers on Seq@K as an evaluation metric, and as a result, considers situation where the feedback is provided under privileged information about the correct answer or grading criteria. This reflects the common setting where users of an agent provides information on how its attempts were inadequate. Other recent work evaluate this ability by introducing novel tasks. RefineBench (Lee et al., 2025) introduces a new set of tasks with checklist-based evaluation, and finds that self-refinement yields little improvement while targeted feedback drives frontier models close to saturation. ICPC-Eval’s Refine@K (Xu et al., 2025) measures revision from execution feedback in competitive programming. Instead of constructing new tasks, we demonstrate that on existing benchmarks and settings the community already considers, the Seq@K evaluation protocol already reveals insights on model performance rankings and novel cost-performance Pareto frontiers. These insights demonstrate how Seq@K is an important metric to report alongside Pass@K on benchmarks or settings where iterative refinement is expected in practice.

Multi-turn and agentic evaluation.

Agent benchmarks such as SWE-bench, WebArena, and τ\tau-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025) and multi-turn evaluations such as MINT (Wang et al., 2024) score models over long interactions with tools and environments. In these settings, success depends jointly on planning, tool use, state tracking, and the use of feedback. Seq@K isolates the last of these, where each piece of feedback provides information on the entire attempt. Hence, differences in Seq@K reflect how models revise their attempts and not how they navigate an environment.

3 Seq@K Evaluation Protocol

Both Pass@K and Seq@K evaluate whether a model succeeds at least once within an attempt budget of KK, but they differ in whether candidate draws are independent or generated through iterative refinement from feedback. Independent sampling generates each candidate from a static task prompt, whereas sequential evaluation conditions each revision on preceding candidate responses and feedback. We mathematically formulate these metrics as follows.

Let 𝒟={xi}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a benchmark of NN tasks, where xix_{i} is the initial prompt for task ii. Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denote the candidate solution space. Each task xix_{i} is paired with a verifier Vi:𝒴→{0,1}V_{i}:\mathcal{Y}\to\{0,1\} indicating whether a candidate y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} passes the success requirement. The verifier may be an LLM if the evaluation protocol of the benchmark requires an LLM grader. A model with parameters θ\theta induces a conditional decoding distribution πθ(⋅∣c)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c) over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} given an input context cc. We call this model the actor, to distinguish it from the models that write feedback (critics) or grade attempts (graders).

Pass@K.

Under independent sampling, context is restricted strictly to the original task prompt (c=xic=x_{i}). For each task xix_{i}, the model independently draws KK candidate solutions Yi,1,…,Yi,K∼πθ(⋅∣xi)Y_{i,1},\dots,Y_{i,K}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i}). A task succeeds if at least one candidate passes the verifier ViV_{i}. The Pass@K metric computes the expected success rate across the benchmark:

Pass@K=1N∑i=1N𝔼Yi,1,…,Yi,K∼πθ(⋅∣xi)[max1≤t≤KVi(Yi,t)].\mathrm{Pass@}K=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{Y_{i,1},\dots,Y_{i,K}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i})}\left[\max_{1\leq t\leq K}V_{i}(Y_{i,t})\right]. (1)

Because Vi​(y)∈{0,1}V_{i}(y)\in\{0,1\}, the maximum over attempt steps tt evaluates to 11 if any attempt succeeds and 00 otherwise.

Seq@K.

Under sequential evaluation, attempts are generated iteratively, allowing the prompt context to expand with past candidate responses and environmental feedback. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} denote the space of feedback messages. A feedback mode mm specifies what feedback message the actor receives after a failed attempt (Section 4). The interaction history before attempt tt is Hi,t−1=((Yi,1,Fi,1),…,(Yi,t−1,Fi,t−1))H_{i,t-1}=\big((Y_{i,1},F_{i,1}),\dots,(Y_{i,t-1},F_{i,t-1})\big), with Hi,0=∅H_{i,0}=\emptyset.

At attempt t∈{1,…,K}t\in\{1,\dots,K\}, the model samples Yi,t∼πθ(⋅∣xi,Hi,t−1)Y_{i,t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i},H_{i,t-1}). If the attempt fails (Vi​(Yi,t)=0V_{i}(Y_{i,t})=0), the environment returns feedback Fi,t∈ℱF_{i,t}\in\mathcal{F} according to the feedback mode mm, which is appended to Hi,t−1H_{i,t-1} for the next turn. If the attempt succeeds (Vi​(Yi,t)=1V_{i}(Y_{i,t})=1), interaction terminates early. We call an attempt with t≥2t\geq 2, which is conditioned on earlier attempts and feedback, a revision or a revised attempt. Let τi\tau_{i} denote the resulting sequential trajectory, and let Pθ,m,i(K)(⋅∣xi)P_{\theta,m,i}^{(K)}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) denote the joint distribution over trajectories induced by the model, feedback mode mm, and budget KK. The Seq@K metric evaluates the expected trajectory success rate:

Seq@K=1N∑i=1N𝔼τi∼Pθ,m,i(K)(⋅∣xi)[max1≤t≤KVi(Yi,t)].\mathrm{Seq@}K=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{i}\sim P_{\theta,m,i}^{(K)}(\cdot\mid x_{i})}\left[\max_{1\leq t\leq K}V_{i}(Y_{i,t})\right]. (2)

When a trajectory halts early upon success, the maximum is evaluated over generated attempts within budget KK. Unlike Pass@K, successive candidate attempts in Seq@K are not independent draws from a static prompt; each revision depends directly on previous attempts and feedback.

Feedback Modes and Protocol Dependencies.

The Seq@K metric forms a family of feedback-conditioned evaluations indexed by the feedback mode mm. A numerical Seq@K value is well-defined only after specifying feedback mode mm alongside the benchmark task split, verifier, prompt builder, decoding hyperparameters, and attempt budget.

4 Experimental Design

We evaluate 77 benchmark variants spanning instruction following, rubric-graded generation, and executable code synthesis. Table 1 outlines these benchmarks alongside their experimental configurations and the Results sections that use them. Each empirical comparison uses actors, task splits, and protocol settings drawn from this central collection, with matching criteria and remaining protocol differences specified in the appendix. Detailed definitions for all benchmarks, success criteria, task screening procedures, and decoding parameters are provided in Appendix A.

Feedback modes.

We compare independent parallel sampling (Pass@K) against three distinct sequential feedback modes, categorized by the signal provided to the actor following a failed attempt:

  • ∙\bullet

    Binary Feedback: Provides only an outcome pass/fail verdict. This mode evaluates whether knowing that a candidate failed provides sufficient leverage to guide subsequent revision.

  • ∙\bullet

    Raw Verifier Feedback: Returns direct environment or evaluator diagnostics—including execution stack traces, failed test assertions, or rubric item breakdowns. This mode tests whether models can interpret and act upon evaluator diagnostics.

  • ∙\bullet

    LLM Critic Feedback: Uses a language model to generate targeted critique from the candidate response and the information supplied to the critic. The critic role can be fulfilled by the actor model itself or another language model. We systematically vary the critic’s context, including whether it has explicit access to underlying grading rubrics.

Feedback mode specifies the information boundary maintained during revision rounds. For example, raw test diagnostics can expose test failures and expected outputs, whereas rubric-aware critics use evaluation rubrics to generate guidance for the actor.

Having established the benchmark coverage, feedback channels, and evaluation protocols, we next present our empirical findings on how Seq@K reshapes model selection, exposes revision dynamics, and quantifies feedback utility across these systems.

5 Results

We structure our empirical investigation around three core questions: (1) Does evaluating models under sequential feedback alter model selection and cost–performance trade-offs? (2) How do revisions unfold across successive feedback turns? (3) What properties of the feedback channel determine whether an attempt succeeds or stalls?

5.1 Model-selection under Seq@K

5.1.1 More performant and efficient model selection with Seq@K

A model’s ranking under static, single-attempt evaluation (Pass@5) can diverge significantly from its ranking under multi-turn sequential evaluation (Seq@5). As shown in Figure 1, Sonnet climbs from the bottom rank under independent sampling on AdvancedIF to the top tied group after sequential feedback, with similar order inversions occurring on CLBench DKR. Given this disparity, the practical question is whether evaluating the intended feedback loop helps us choose a better model with limited calibration spending.

Selection test. We simulate a practitioner who picks an actor on a few calibration tasks and then deploys it with sequential feedback on new tasks. We compare picking by Pass@5 with picking by Seq@K at a shorter depth (K=3K=3 or 44). Since each sequential attempt carries the earlier attempts and feedback in its context, Seq@K can be more costly. We therefore also record the calibration cost. Each candidate actor runs three times on the same calibration tasks at T=0.7T=0.7, and we average its success over the three repetitions. We pick the actor with the highest score in calibration tasks (breaking ties uniformly at random), and evaluate it under raw-verifier-feedback (with details on failed tests) Seq@5 on held-out tasks. Selection loss is the main metric we use to evaluate the performance of selection process, which is the held-out score gap between the picked actor and the best candidate.

We evenly split the 4545 MBPP Pro tasks and the 4040 HumanEval Pro tasks (Appendix A.3) into two fixed groups per benchmark, group A and B. We calibrate on A and evaluate on B, and vice versa. For a given calibration and evaluation group, we repeatedly draw nn tasks for each n∈[20]n\in[20] from the calibration group, with the evaluation task set held fixed across draws and calibration sizes. Figure 2 reports selection loss and calibration cost averaged over draws and both directions, with each direction weighted by the size of its evaluation group. Table 2 reports n=10n=10. Confidence intervals come from bootstrap (Appendix B.1).

Finding. Calibrating with Seq@3 or Seq@4picks significantly better actors for sequential deployment than calibrating with Pass@5, at similar or lower cost (Figure 2 and Table 2). The gain is largest on HumanEval Pro, where actors that look similar under Pass@5 differ widely under Seq@5 (Table 3).

5.1.2 Pass@K can overstate or understate performance gaps

The cost of selecting a worse actors depends on how far apart the candidate actors are in performance (Table 3). On AdvancedIF, the gap between the best and worst actor is 33.333.3 points under Pass@5 but only 6.76.7 points under Seq@5 with raw verifier feedback. This is one example where, as long as proper feedback is provided, the performance gap between actors is not as large. HumanEval Pro is a contrasting example, where actors differ even more with feedback that gives details on failed tests (10.8→51.710.8\rightarrow 51.7 points from Pass@5 to Seq@5). Here, actors differ in how well they use the feedback in their next attempts, and the tasks are ones where this ability matters. The average gap over all model pairs moves in the same directions, suggesting that this is a prevalent pattern in each benchmark. On MBPP Pro, the gap also widens. These cases show that Pass@K can significantly understate or overstate the differences between actors, so where sequential interaction is expected, Seq@K should be considered instead.

5.1.3 Seq@K reveals better Pareto-optimal choices

In practice, one could deploy an agent for KK parallel attempts as represented by Pass@K. Seq@K represents the alternative of revising with feedback for up to a predetermined KK attempts. While each sequential attempt carries more context from previous sessions, they also tend to have earlier successes from incorporating feedback. This motivates us to explore the cost-performance Pareto frontier of both protocols.

Figure 3 shows the Pareto frontier of each protocol over two benchmarks, all actors, and K=1K=1 to 55. Seq@K often reveals a better Pareto frontier than Pass@K, with higher success for the same cost. The difference is largest on DKR, where independent sampling solves at most about 14%14\% of tasks, while sequential feedback reaches 50%50\% (Opus 4.7 at K=5K=5).

5.1.4 Seq@K tracks a distinct capability signal from Pass@K

The previous results show the operational implications of Seq@K for choosing models. We complement them with a more direct study of how Seq@K tracks a different capability from Pass@K. At first glance, the two metrics are somewhat correlated. Over 2626 model–benchmark pairs, Pass@5 and Seq@5 have Spearman correlation +0.68+0.68 (Figure 4a). This is because the two protocols have approximately the same success rate on the first attempt, which reflects the actor’s one-shot capability on the task. To control for this, we measure instead how much attempts 2 to 5 add under each protocol:

Δ​Pass@K=Pass@K−Pass@1,Δ​Seq@K=Seq@K−Seq@1.{\Delta\text{Pass@K}=\text{Pass@K}-\text{Pass@1},\qquad\Delta\text{Seq@K}=\text{Seq@K}-\text{Seq@1}.}

With the first attempt removed, the correlation drops to −0.08-0.08 (Figure 4b). That is, how much a model gains from more independent samples says little about how much it gains from feedback. Hence, the iterative refinement capability that Seq@K evaluation aims to track is distinct from what Seq@K captures.

5.2 Seq@K reveals when and how revisions succeed

The numerical results on success rates earlier do not show when revisions succeed or how an actor responds to feedback. But the rate at which agents’ revisions succeed and how well the revisions address the feedback directly impacts the usability of agentic systems. In this section, we examine when revised attempts yield gains and failure modes in agents’ revision patterns.

5.2.1 Revision timing distinguishes front-loaded from distributed gains

Models with similar Seq@5 can follow distinct revision trajectories across turns. This profile matters when deployment limits the number of revision turns. To characterize this behavior, we analyze how performance improvements distribute across revision turns. For any model exhibiting net improvement (Δ​Seq@5>0\Delta\text{Seq@5}>0), we compute the Early-Gain Share (EGS) and Last-Gain Share (LGS):

EGS=Seq@2−Seq@1Δ​Seq@5,LGS=Seq@5−Seq@4Δ​Seq@5.{\mathrm{EGS}=\frac{\text{Seq@2}-\text{Seq@1}}{\Delta\text{Seq@5}},\qquad\mathrm{LGS}=\frac{\text{Seq@5}-\text{Seq@4}}{\Delta\text{Seq@5}}.}

The early-gain share (EGS) is the fraction of improvement obtained on the first retry. The last-step share (LGS) is the fraction obtained on the final allowed attempt.

We evaluate these metrics using rubric-guided DKR setups across two distinct critic styles: directive feedback (providing explicit actionable revision instructions) and socratic feedback (providing targeted probing questions). Table 4 summarizes the distribution of gains across turns for these configurations. In the selected configurations, Gemini 3 Flash obtains most of its gain on the first retry with the highest EGS, which may be preferable for settings where earlier revisions are preferred. On the other hand, a non-zero LGS like that of Opus 4.7 or DeepSeek V4 Pro indicates potential gains from more repeated attempts.

5.2.2 Revisions do not always address the feedback

We next examine whether provided feedback are addressed in agents’ next attempts. Some unhelpful revisions are easy to identify since the next attempt entails the same answer as before with no changes. In coding, we find such examples with Qwen3 Coder Flash and DeepSeek V3.2: 48%48\% and 6%6\% of revised attempts respectively are exactly the same attempt as before without modifications, whereas Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3 Flash never submit an unmodified revised attempt (Figure 5a).

Other unhelpful revisions update the attempts but nonetheless fail to address the feedback. Unlike the aforementioned failure mode that can be programmatically identified, finding cases where revisions took place but are ineffective takes manual inspection. Below, we show 2 of the 14 examples we identify (Examples 5.2.2 and 5.2.2) and more in Appendix E.

Since manually going through all revisions is not feasible, we employ a similar approach to GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026): we use the 14 examples to develop a prompt, and use Claude Opus 5.5 to annotate all tasks in the four benchmarks (AdvancedIF, CLBench DKR, HumanEval Pro, and MBPP Pro) on attempts that contain revisions. For each feedback, the annotator judges whether the revised attempt satisfies it. A revision is unhelpful if it satisfies none of the remaining requests, addresses some of the feedback if it fully or partly satisfies at least one, and addresses all of the feedback if it fully satisfies every one. Across 842842 revisions, we find that 186186 (22%22\%) are unhelpful, 289289 (34%34\%) address some, and 367367 (44%44\%) address all of the feedback (Appendix D.2).

In Figure 5b, we further show how unhelpful revisions impact task successes in the sequential setting. First, as expected, unhelpful revisions almost never succeed in the next attempt. Success rises when some of the feedback are deemed partially addressed. However, addressing all of the feedback is not enough and many such revisions still fail; this is because the revisions can break a criterion that passed before as it addresses the current feedback. This failure mode is particularly pronounced in the DKR and AdvancedIF benchmarks, where success requires meeting multiple criteria, and less so the case in coding benchmarks.

5.3 Seq@K diagnoses the feedback loop

So far, we examined how agents perform under Seq@K and respond to feedback. In this section, we look at the feedback itself: what information it contains, whether the critic knows what is being graded, and how much of the previous attempts the agent sees.

5.3.1 Effectiveness of binary feedback depends on the benchmark

Binary feedback only tells the agent that its attempt failed, without saying which requirements are not met. In DKR, binary feedback is largely unhelpful. To measure this, we take the requirements that the first attempt fails and measure the fraction of them fixed in the best later attempt (the attempt that satisfies the most requirements, taking the latest one if tied). We call this fraction criterion repair. In Table 5, we compare independent retries, binary feedback, and critiques written with and without access to the grading rubric. Binary feedback and critiques without the rubric repair about as many criteria as independent retries, whereas critiques with the rubric repair many more. Binary feedback is similarly unhelpful for DeepSeek V3.2 and Qwen3 Coder Flash in coding, where it changes Seq@5 by at most 3.33.3 points from Pass@5 (Appendix F.2).

On the other hand, binary feedback is helpful for Sonnet 4.6 in coding, since Sonnet can reason on its own about why its code failed when it was run. Compared to Pass@5, Seq@5 with binary feedback is 1717 to 2626 points higher for Sonnet on HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro (Appendix F.2), whereas in DKR it is only 11 point higher on average across six models. Overall, this shows that effectiveness of different feedback type is dependent on both benchmark and model-capability. Therefore, in designing feedback harnesses around models, practitioners may benefit more from highlighting criteria that agents would otherwise not come up on their own from reasoning.

5.3.2 Summarizing the history can lower sequential success

In Seq@K, the prompt for each attempt includes the latest feedback and the previous attempts. When we replace the previous attempts with a summary, performance changes little on AdvancedIF and coding but drops on the other benchmarks, most consistently on HealthBench (Table 6). How the history is kept is therefore part of the protocol and should be reported along with Seq@K. Details are provided in Appendix F.3.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

We introduced Seq@K, which measures whether a model solves a task within KK attempts when it receives feedback after each failed attempt. Model rankings, gaps between actors, and cost-performance frontiers can all differ between Seq@K and Pass@K, so choosing a model by Pass@K can pick the wrong one for an agent that revises from feedback. Seq@K trajectories also show when models gain and how revisions fail, for example by ignoring the feedback or by breaking requirements that passed before. Finally, Seq@K helps diagnose the feedback loop itself. We find how much feedback helps depends on what it tells the agent, whether the critic knows what is being graded, and how the history is kept. Practitioners building agentic systems around a feedback loop should choose models with Seq@K under the feedback the agent will receive, since Pass@K may favor a model that does not use that feedback well.

Appendix A Benchmark and Setup Details

Table 7 lists the benchmarks and when an attempt counts as a success. The rest of this appendix explains how feedback, history, and grading are set up (Appendix A.1), gives the exact prompts and feedback used in coding (Appendix A.2), and lists the coding tasks we exclude (Appendix A.3).

A.1 Feedback, history, and grading

Feedback.

Binary feedback tells the actor only that its attempt failed. Raw verifier feedback on AdvancedIF gives the verdict for each rubric item. Rubric-aware critics see the grading rubric when they write feedback, and rubric-blind critics do not. In coding, feedback either says that the code failed (binary) or shows the failed tests (test details), and Appendix A.2 gives the exact text. Raw verifier feedback and test details show the actor part of what is graded, so Seq@K under these modes measures success with that information.

History.

By default, the prompt for each sequential attempt contains the task, a note on the attempt number, and every earlier attempt with its feedback. In the summarized-history runs, a summary replaces the earlier attempts (Appendix F.3).

Temperature and repetitions.

The main comparisons use T=0.7T=0.7, and we do not tune the temperature. Coding runs are repeated three times, labeled seeds 1–3. Some coding runs in the history comparison use T=0T=0.

Grading.

Unless stated otherwise, AdvancedIF attempts are graded by Sonnet 4.6. CLBench attempts are graded by GPT-5.4, with GPT-5.2 as a fallback when GPT-5.4 refuses to grade.

Confidence intervals.

We compute 95%95\% intervals by resampling tasks with replacement. Each resampled task keeps the results of every actor and protocol on it, so both sides of a comparison are always computed on the same tasks. Coding scores are averaged over the three repetitions before resampling. The model-selection analysis resamples tasks within each calibration and evaluation group (Appendix B.1).

A.2 Coding prompts and feedback

Both coding benchmarks use the prompt below. The fields in braces are replaced with the benchmark’s problem statements. The prompt does not contain the reference solution or the tests. Under Pass@K, every attempt receives this prompt unchanged, and all KK attempts are generated. Under Seq@K, the run stops at the first passing attempt.

You are solving a Python code generation task.

There are two related functions:
1. Base function: solve the simpler base problem.
2. Main function: solve the harder problem by using or building on the base function.

Write complete Python code that defines all required functions.
Do not import unnecessary packages.
Do not include explanations outside the code.

Base problem:
‘‘‘python
{base_problem}
‘‘‘

Main problem:
‘‘‘python
{main_problem}
‘‘‘

Return only the Python code.

Under Seq@K, the task is followed by a note on the attempt number and then by every earlier attempt with its feedback, separated by blank lines. On the first attempt, the note is:

This is attempt 1 of {K}. If this attempt does not pass, you will receive feedback and can revise it on the remaining attempts.

On later attempts, it is:

This is attempt {t} of {K}. Review your previous attempt(s) and the feedback below, then provide an improved answer.

Each earlier attempt ii is added in order as follows. The whole prompt is sent as one user message. A variant of the note leaves out the number of attempts and keeps the rest.

<PreviousAttempt {i}>
{actor_output_i}
</PreviousAttempt {i}>

<Feedback {i}>
{feedback_i}
</Feedback {i}>

Binary feedback is: “Your previous solution failed the hidden tests. Please revise the code.” Test-detail feedback begins with “Your previous solution failed.” and “Failed test details:”. It then shows up to two failed tests, each with the function call, the expected output, and the actual output, or the error message when these are missing. Each field is cut at 300300 characters. The feedback ends with “Use this feedback to fix the general logic. Do not hard-code these cases.” and “Return only the revised Python code.” If the tests report no individual failures, the feedback is the raw test output. Some T=0T=0 runs use error-summary feedback instead, which lists up to three failed tests with the test name, the error type, and a short summary, without the expected output.

A.3 Excluded coding tasks

In 1515 of the 100100 coding tasks, the tests call a function that the prompt never names, so an attempt can only pass if it guesses the name or learns it from the feedback. These are 1010 HumanEval Pro tasks (dataset IDs 3,5,14,20,21,22,28,46,63,1123,5,14,20,21,22,28,46,63,112) and 55 MBPP Pro tasks (dataset IDs 19,41,47,69,7519,41,47,69,75). Among the HumanEval Pro tasks, seven give a base-function signature that does not match the tests, and three leave out the main function’s definition. We find these tasks by checking the function names called in the tests against the names in the prompt, so other kinds of defects can remain.

The coding comparisons and the model-selection analysis exclude these tasks, which leaves 4545 MBPP Pro and 4040 HumanEval Pro tasks. The history comparison uses all 5050 tasks of each benchmark (Appendix F.3).

Appendix B Model Selection Details

This appendix gives the details of the selection test in Section 5.1 and of the gaps between actors in Table 3.

B.1 Selection test

Runs.

The candidates are Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek V3.2, Gemini 3 Flash, and Qwen3 Coder Flash. Each actor runs three times under Pass@K and three times under Seq@K with test-detail feedback, at T=0.7T=0.7 and K=5K=5, on the 4545 MBPP Pro and 4040 HumanEval Pro tasks. This gives 4848 runs and 2,0402{,}040 trajectories. Seq@3 and Seq@4 are read from the first three or four attempts of the K=5K=5 runs, whose prompts say that five attempts are available.

Selection and loss.

On each set of calibration tasks, we score every actor by its success averaged over the three repetitions and pick the highest, breaking ties at random. The picked actor is evaluated by its test-detail Seq@5 on the evaluation tasks, averaged over the three repetitions. Let CC be the calibration tasks, EE the evaluation tasks, ℳ\mathcal{M} the candidate actors, D5​(m,E)D_{5}(m,E) the Seq@5 of actor mm on EE, and m^​(C)\widehat{m}(C) the actor picked on CC. The selection loss is

L⁡(C,E)=maxm∈ℳ⁡D5​(m,E)−D5​(m^​(C),E).L(C,E)=\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}D_{5}(m,E)-D_{5}(\widehat{m}(C),E).

The evaluation tasks are never used for picking. The loss is zero when the picked actor is the best on EE, and it can be positive even under Seq@5 calibration, because the best actor on CC need not be the best on EE. The best score on EE is the same for every calibration metric, so a lower loss means a higher Seq@5 for the picked actor. The Gain in Table 2 is this difference.

Cost.

The calibration cost is the sum of the actor API charges over the four actors, the calibration tasks, and the three repetitions. Coding has no judge or critic, so this is the full model cost. Under both protocols, a trajectory is charged up to its first success or its last allowed attempt. The cost does not include running the tests. We report the mean cost and do not cap the spending on any single calibration set.

Calibration and evaluation groups.

We split MBPP Pro into groups of 2222 and 2323 tasks and HumanEval Pro into two groups of 2020. We calibrate on one group, evaluate on the whole other group, and then swap. In each direction, we draw 128,000128{,}000 random orders of the calibration tasks and use the first nn tasks of each order, so every calibration metric sees the same tasks. We chose this number by increasing it from 2,0002{,}000 until two independent sets of draws agreed on the gain of Seq@3 over Pass@5 at n=10n=10 within 0.10.1 points. The two directions are averaged, weighted by the size of their evaluation group.

Confidence intervals.

We compute 95%95\% intervals by resampling tasks with replacement 2,0002{,}000 times. Each resample draws tasks within each group and keeps the results of every actor, protocol, and repetition on a task together. On each resample, we rerun the selection over 200200 random orders of the calibration tasks in each direction. Using 400400 orders instead changes the interval endpoints by at most 0.30.3 points. At n=20n=20, HumanEval Pro calibrates on all 2020 tasks of its group, so the order of the tasks does not matter and only the resampling adds variation.

Seq@3 and Seq@4.

Table 8 gives the gain and the cost relative to Pass@5 at n=10n=10. We chose Seq@3 before running the analysis and added Seq@4 after seeing the Seq@3 results. All four gain intervals exclude zero. Seq@3 and Seq@4 cost 0.940.94 and 1.061.06 times as much as Pass@5 on MBPP Pro, and 0.790.79 and 0.920.92 times as much on HumanEval Pro. Three of the four cost-ratio intervals include one, and on MBPP Pro, Seq@3 costs more than Pass@5 on 28%28\% of the drawn calibration sets.

Scope.

The gain of Seq@3 over Pass@5 stays positive under all twenty other ways of splitting the tasks into two groups, on both benchmarks. These tasks are also used elsewhere in the paper. Seq@3 and Seq@4 come from runs that were told five attempts were available, so runs told they have three or four attempts may behave differently. We compare against Pass@5 only, not against every way of spending the same budget on independent samples.

B.2 Gaps between actors

Table 3 reports two gaps for each protocol: the difference between the best and worst actor, and the average absolute difference over all pairs of actors. Table 9 adds 95%95\% intervals for the change in each gap from Pass@5 to Seq@5. Each bootstrap draw resamples tasks, keeping all actors and both protocols of a task together, and recomputes both gaps. We use 2,0002{,}000 draws for the best–worst gap and 10,00010{,}000 for the all-pairs gap. Coding scores are averaged over the three repetitions before resampling, and AdvancedIF has one run per actor. The best–worst gap depends on which two actors are at the ends, so it moves more when actors are close. The all-pairs gap is less sensitive to this.

Appendix C Cost Frontiers and Score Correlations

C.1 Cost of each protocol

Figure 3 compares the cost and success of Pass@K and Seq@K for K=1K=1 to 55 without running new attempts. For each actor and task, we take the recorded K=5K=5 runs of both protocols, go through their attempts in the original order, and stop at the first passing attempt or after attempt KK. The cost of a task is the API charge of the attempts up to that point. Under Pass@K the actor never sees feedback, and the verdict is used only to decide when to stop. Each point in the figure is the mean cost per task and the success rate of one actor at one KK.

On AdvancedIF, the cost includes the actor and the judge. On DKR, it includes the actor only.

All actors in a panel are scored on the same tasks: 3030 AdvancedIF tasks for seven actors, and 2828 DKR tasks for six actors. On DKR, Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.2 get directive feedback from themselves as critic, and the other actors get socratic feedback from GPT-5.2. Table 10 gives the DKR scores on these 2828 tasks. Other DKR tables use 3030 tasks per actor, so their scores differ slightly. A point is on a protocol’s frontier if no other point of that protocol reaches the same or higher success at a lower cost. The cost axis is logarithmic.

C.2 Correlation between protocols

Figure 4 uses 2626 model–benchmark pairs: AdvancedIF (7), CLBench DKR (7), HealthBench (6), CLBench RSA (3), and ResearchRubrics (3). Coding is not included. Within a pair, both protocols use the same actor, temperature (T=0.7T=0.7), K=5K=5, grader, and tasks. When a pair has several sequential runs, we use the non-binary feedback setting with the full history that has the highest Seq@5. Because this choice is made on the same tasks, the Seq@5 values are optimistic. Repeated runs of the same setting are pooled. Table 11 gives the scores of every pair.

Over the 2626 pairs, Pass@5 and Seq@5 have Spearman correlation +0.68+0.68 and Pearson correlation +0.81+0.81. For the gains Δ​Pass@5\Delta\text{Pass@5} and Δ​Seq@5\Delta\text{Seq@5}, the Spearman correlation is −0.08-0.08 (95%95\% interval [−0.47,+0.31][-0.47,+0.31]) and the Pearson correlation is −0.04-0.04 ([−0.38,+0.26][-0.38,+0.26]). The intervals come from 2,0002{,}000 bootstrap draws of the 2626 pairs, which treat the pairs as independent although actors and benchmarks recur. Eleven pairs have no gain under Pass@5.

Appendix D Revision Dynamics Details

D.1 Success by attempt

Table 12 gives Seq@K for K=1K=1 to 55 on the DKR runs of Table 4, with 3030 tasks per actor. Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.2 get directive feedback from themselves as critic, and DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Qwen3.6 Max get socratic feedback from GPT-5.2. Since the feedback differs across actors, the rows do not compare actors under the same feedback.

When an actor revise successfully also depends on the feedback setup. In two other DKR runs with a different critic, grader, and note on the attempt number, Qwen3.6 Max has an EGS of 0.570.57 and 0.500.50, compared with 0.200.20 in Table 4. Final success changes as well. In runs where the actor critiques itself, GPT-5.4 grades, and the prompt leaves out the number of attempts, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Qwen3.6 27B reach Seq@5 of 0.3330.333, 0.2330.233, and 0.2670.267. EGS and LGS therefore describe an actor under a given feedback setup, not the actor alone.

D.2 Annotation of revisions

This section gives the details of the revision annotation in Section 5.2.2: which revisions we annotate, how the annotator labels them, and how often two annotators agree.

Settings.

We reuse recorded runs from four settings (Table 13). Each setting fixes the feedback, critic, grader, temperature (T=0.7T=0.7), and history, so actors within a setting differ only in the actor model and seed. A revision is one step from attempt tt, through the feedback on it, to attempt t+1t{+}1. A trajectory is included if its first attempt failed.

Task split.

Tasks were split at random (seed 2026092520260925), so every run and attempt of a task falls on one side. The prompt was developed on the 1414 audited examples (Appendix E) and 1111 random tasks (44 AdvancedIF, 33 DKR, 33 HumanEval Pro, 11 MBPP Pro). The two AdvancedIF settings share 1616 of their held-out tasks, giving 102102 distinct tasks: 6060 AdvancedIF, 2323 DKR, 1111 HumanEval Pro, and 88 MBPP Pro. For coding we annotate 2020 random tasks out of 100100; four of them have interface defects (Appendix A.3). Figure 5b excludes the 6262 revisions on those four tasks and the 131131 revisions whose feedback contains no valid request, leaving 842842.

Annotation.

For each revision the annotator sees the task prompt, the rubric text, earlier attempts and feedback, attempt tt, the feedback on it, attempt t+1t{+}1, and a line diff. The actor, run, and all verdicts are hidden, and an annotation batch contains at most one revision per trajectory. The annotator lists each change the feedback requests and labels it valid, interpretive, unclear, or invalid (for example, a test that contradicts the prompt). It then records whether attempt t+1t{+}1 satisfies each request (yes, partly, or no), with a verbatim quote as evidence. A request also counts as satisfied when attempt tt already met it and attempt t+1t{+}1 still does. Whether a revision is unhelpful, addresses some, or addresses all of the feedback is computed from these labels after dropping invalid requests.

To develop the prompt, Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet independently labeled 6868 revisions from the development tasks (1616 random revisions per setting and the two example AdvancedIF trajectories). The prompt was revised where they disagreed, then frozen before any held-out revision was annotated and before any verdict after attempt 1 was read.

Reliability.

Claude Sonnet independently annotated a stratified 15%15\% of held-out revisions (165165). The two annotators agree on this category for 80%80\% of them (κ=0.73\kappa=0.73); agreement is lowest in DKR (κ=0.53\kappa=0.53). A third blind Claude Opus pass resolved the 6969 disagreements; using its labels leaves the conclusions unchanged. All 2,0292{,}029 non-empty evidence quotes occur verbatim in the revised attempt. These are LLM labels, not human annotations, and three of the actors are Claude models.

Broken criteria.

For the counts of revisions that address all feedback yet fail, a criterion counts as broken if it passed at attempt tt, fails at attempt t+1t{+}1, and no annotated request refers to it. Requests the annotator did not tie to a rubric item are treated as unmentioned, so these counts may slightly overstate breakage. Intervals in Figure 5b are 95%95\% percentiles over 4,0004{,}000 resamples of tasks within each setting.

Appendix E Qualitative Analysis of Revision Trajectories

E.1 How we chose and read the examples

We read 3131 trajectories (115115 attempts) on 1414 tasks from AdvancedIF, CLBench DKR, HealthBench, and HumanEval Pro. We started from cases we noticed during the study, added runs of the same tasks under other feedback, and added one coding pair. Section 5.2.2 shows two of these examples (Examples 5.2.2 and 5.2.2), and this appendix shows two more. Table 14 lists every trajectory we used. The examples show patterns of revision, not how often each pattern occurs. Appendix D.2 annotates revisions on 102102 other tasks.

For each trajectory we read the task, the attempts, the feedback, and the verdicts. A trajectory stops at its first passing attempt. RiR_{i} is the rubric’s own item number. Quotes are shortened to the relevant part. A contrast run starts from its own first attempt, so it does not show the same attempt under different feedback.

E.2 Revisions that do not act on the feedback: a tested function that is never defined

This example shows an actor whose revisions do not act on clear feedback, including resubmitting the same code (Figure 5a). Both actors get the same task and the same test-detail feedback, and only one of them fixes its code. The task is one of the defective tasks of Appendix A.3: the tests call a function that the prompt never names, so the feedback is the only way to learn the name. We chose this pair by taking the first task, by task ID, among the 1717 seed-1 tasks where both actors failed the first attempt, Sonnet 4.6 later passed, and Qwen3 Coder Flash never did.

Example E.1. Qwen3 Coder Flash under test-detail feedback, with Sonnet 4.6 on the same task and feedback as contrast.

E.3 Revisions that break requirements that passed before: podcast review

This example shows how a revision that addresses the current feedback can break a requirement that passed before (Figure 5b). These podcast runs use socratic feedback with different critics and graders. They are separate from the directive runs for Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.2 in Table 4.

Example E.2. Podcast compliance: GPT-5.2, with the other actors’ failed-requirement sets as contrast.

GPT-5.2 critiques itself and is graded by GPT-5.4. The number of failed requirements falls from 44 to 11, but which requirements fail keeps changing. R16R_{16} passes from attempt 4, although the grader is more lenient about the labels than in earlier attempts. Opus 4.7 also critiques itself and is graded by GPT-5.4. Its second attempt adds a severity legend and labels each issue, which fixes R16R_{16}, and the remaining failure moves to R8R_{8} and then R9R_{9} before it passes. Qwen3.6 Max and Qwen3.6 27B use GPT-5.2 as critic and grader, and both pass at attempt 3. DeepSeek V4 Pro passes on its first attempt.

E.4 List of trajectories

Table 14 lists every trajectory we used, including first-attempt successes and runs used only as contrasts. Unless noted, the non-coding runs use seed 42, T=0.7T=0.7, and K=5K=5. Opus 4.7’s SideHustleBot run uses K=3K=3, and Gemini 3 Flash’s self-judge run on tinnitus uses T=0T=0. The coding pair uses seed 1, T=0.7T=0.7, full history, and test-detail feedback. In AdvancedIF, blind critique means that the actor critiques itself without the rubric. In the DKR podcast runs, Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.2 critique themselves, and DeepSeek V4 Pro and the Qwen models get feedback from GPT-5.2. The dog-summary and SpartanAI runs also use GPT-5.2 as critic. In HealthBench, self-judge feedback comes from the actor and judge feedback comes from the grader. Raw and binary feedback use no critic.

Appendix F Feedback Loop Details

F.1 Criterion repair in DKR

Table 15 breaks down the criterion repair of Table 5 by actor. Each actor uses the 3030 tasks it has under all four conditions. For each task, we choose the attempt that passes the most criteria, taking the latest one if tied. Criterion repair is the share of criteria that fail in the first attempt but pass in the chosen attempt. Regression is the share of criteria that pass in the first attempt but fail in the chosen attempt. Pooled rates add up the criterion counts over actors before dividing. Each condition has its own first attempt, so the number of failed criteria differs across conditions. Regressions in attempts other than the chosen one are not counted. Binary feedback repairs 2.12.1 points fewer criteria than independent sampling, with a 95%95\% interval of [−11.5,+5.8][-11.5,+5.8] from 10,00010{,}000 resamples of the tasks (Appendix A.1).

F.2 Binary feedback in coding

Table 16 gives the coding scores used in Table 3 and Section 5.3. Each cell averages three runs at T=0.7T=0.7 on the 4545 MBPP Pro or 4040 HumanEval Pro tasks.

F.3 Summarized history

Each unit is a pair of trajectories on the same task, one with a summarized history and one with the full history. The two trajectories come from two runs with the same benchmark, actor, feedback, budget, grader, prompt variant, seed, and temperature, and at least 3030 tasks in common. There are 5757 such run pairs, which give 2,5202{,}520 trajectory pairs. Table 17 reports the average change in success rate over the trajectory pairs of each benchmark. Unlike the other coding analyses, the coding rows use all 5050 tasks of each benchmark, including the defective tasks of Appendix A.3.
